name: CBT for BDD

lead: CBT for BDD is a structured psychotherapy for people intensely preoccupied with a perceived flaw in their appearance. The payoff is less time and distress spent on the flaw and a steadier, more confident self-image. It is the best-studied psychological treatment for the condition.

Sessions combine education about BDD, challenging appearance-related beliefs, exposure to feared situations while holding back rituals like mirror checking or reassurance seeking, and in some programs mindfulness and attention retraining. A 2016 meta-analysis of randomized trials and a 2019 trial against supportive psychotherapy examined its effect on BDD symptoms, and it has been tested in adolescents and in app-based formats. Trials measure symptoms, not looks.

paras: People work with a trained therapist in regular sessions over several months, practising exposure exercises and tracking rituals between sessions. App-based and digital versions exist for people with limited access to specialists. It is sometimes raised as an alternative or complement to cosmetic procedures.

Therapy has no drug-type side effects, though it can be emotionally demanding because it involves facing feared situations. Access to clinicians trained in BDD is limited, which is one reason digital versions are being studied. A qualified clinician is the route to diagnosis.

angle.text: CBT for BDD uses exposure and response prevention to cut checking behaviours and challenge appearance beliefs, so people spend less energy on perceived flaws and carry themselves with more confidence. It is the best-studied talk therapy for BDD, with trials measuring symptom reduction rather than looks.

lead: Cognitive-behavioral therapy for body dysmorphic disorder (CBT-BDD) is a form of psychotherapy designed for people with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a condition marked by preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance. Treatment typically combines psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, exposure with response prevention (ERP), and in some programs mindfulness and perceptual retraining.[1][2]

It is described in the research literature as the best-studied psychological treatment for BDD.[3] A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examined its effect on validated BDD measures,[3] and a 2019 randomized trial compared therapist-delivered CBT with supportive psychotherapy.[4] Researchers have also tested app-based and digital versions and adolescent programs.[5][6][7]

In looksmaxxing communities, BDD is discussed as a condition that can overlap with appearance-focused self-improvement, and therapy is sometimes raised as an alternative or complement to cosmetic procedures. Wikipedia notes that many people with BDD seek cosmetic or dermatologic treatment that typically does not relieve their distress.[1]

Therapist-delivered, group, app-based with coach support, adolescent programs

paras: BDD is classified in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders group in the DSM-5.[1] People with BDD spend substantial time thinking about a perceived defect and often perform repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking, reassurance seeking, comparing and camouflaging.[1]

A modular CBT program described by Wilhelm and colleagues includes psychoeducation and case formulation, cognitive restructuring, exposure and ritual (response) prevention, and mindfulness and perceptual retraining, according to Wikipedia's summary.[1] In ERP, a person gradually faces feared appearance-related situations, such as going without camouflage, while refraining from the usual checking or avoidance rituals.[3]

A coach-supported smartphone app called Perspectives covers psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, exposure with response prevention, mindfulness, attention retraining and relapse prevention, and was tested in an initial randomized waitlist-controlled trial.[5] An earlier pilot tested a digital CBT service for BDD.[8]
Adolescent-specific CBT has been examined in a case series and in a follow-up of a randomized trial.[6][9]

A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of CBT for BDD, covering published and unpublished trials to November 2015, used validated BDD measures as primary outcomes and depression and insight as secondary outcomes.[3]

A randomized clinical trial published in JAMA Psychiatry in 2019 compared therapist-delivered CBT-BDD with supportive psychotherapy in adults, measuring BDD severity, insight, depression, functioning and quality of life.[4] A separate analysis examined predictors of response to CBT for BDD,[10] and another proposed empirical definitions of treatment response and remission in BDD.[11]

In adolescents, a follow-up study of 26 participants who had received CBT for BDD examined whether treatment gains were maintained over a longer period,[6] and an earlier case series reported on CBT in adolescents.[9]

The coach-supported app trial was a randomized waitlist-controlled study testing usability and efficacy.[5] A Cochrane review of pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy for BDD also covers the topic.[12] An international expert consensus on BDD treatment, published in 2021, synthesised the evidence for psychological and drug treatments.[2]

Wikipedia reports that people with BDD frequently pursue cosmetic surgery or dermatology and that this typically does not relieve their distress; it recommends that cosmetic surgeons and psychiatrists work together to screen for BDD.[1] Prevalence estimates cited there range from about 2-3 percent in the general population to a higher figure in a global meta-analysis, and about 24 percent among people seeking plastic surgery.[1]

timeline.event: DSM-III-R renames the condition body dysmorphic disorder.[1]
DSM-5 places BDD in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders group.[1]
Systematic review and meta-analysis of CBT randomized trials for BDD published.[3]
Randomized trial of CBT-BDD versus supportive psychotherapy published in JAMA Psychiatry.[4]
Initial randomized trial of app-based CBT with coach support published.[5]
